description: Structure links to properties for ionic, covalent and metallic substances, plus nanoparticle uses.
content_html:
Linking Structure to Properties

The physical properties of a substance — its melting point, electrical conductivity, hardness and solubility — depend on the type of bonding and the structure it forms. This is one of the most important relationships in chemistry: understanding the structure allows you to predict and explain the properties. Exam questions very frequently ask you to explain a property in terms of bonding and structure, so you must be able to link every answer back to the forces involved.

Giant Ionic Lattices

Ionic compounds (such as sodium chloride and magnesium oxide) form giant ionic lattices. They have high melting and boiling points because breaking up the lattice requires a large amount of energy to overcome the many strong electrostatic forces between the ions. They do not conduct electricity when solid because the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move. However, they do conduct electricity when molten or when dissolved in water because the ions become free to move and carry charge. Most ionic compounds are soluble in water because water molecules can surround and separate the individual ions. Ionic compounds tend to be brittle: if a force shifts layers of ions so that like charges line up, repulsion between them causes the crystal to shatter.

Key Fact

Ionic compounds: high melting points (strong electrostatic forces in the lattice), conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved (ions must be free to move), do not conduct as solids (ions fixed in the lattice).

Simple Molecular Substances

Simple molecular substances (such as water, oxygen and carbon dioxide) have strong covalent bonds within each molecule but only weak intermolecular forces between molecules. When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, the intermolecular forces are overcome — not the covalent bonds. This gives simple molecular substances low melting and boiling points. They do not conduct electricity in any state because they have no free electrons or ions to carry charge. Larger molecules have more electrons, creating stronger intermolecular forces and therefore higher boiling points. A very common exam error is writing that the covalent bonds are weak — within the molecule, they are strong; the weak forces are those between molecules.

Giant Covalent Structures

Giant covalent structures contain billions of atoms bonded by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure. They have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken to separate the atoms. Carbon forms several giant covalent allotropes:

In diamond, each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds arranged in a rigid tetrahedral lattice. This makes diamond extremely hard and gives it a very high melting point. Diamond does not conduct electricity because all four outer electrons of each carbon are used in covalent bonds — none are free to move.

In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers. The fourth electron on each carbon is delocalised within the layer, allowing graphite to conduct electricity. The layers are held together by weak intermolecular forces and can slide over each other, making graphite soft and useful as a lubricant or pencil material.

Graphene is a single layer of graphite — one atom thick. It is exceptionally strong for its mass, flexible, and an excellent conductor of electricity. It is being researched for uses in electronics, composites and membranes. Fullerenes are hollow carbon molecules. The most studied is buckminsterfullerene (\(C_{60}\)), shaped like a football. Fullerenes are being investigated as drug delivery vehicles and in nanotechnology. Their cage-like structure can trap other molecules.

Key Fact

Graphite conducts electricity because it has delocalised electrons within each layer. Diamond does not conduct because all four of each carbon’s outer electrons are used in covalent bonds. Graphene (a single graphite layer) also conducts. Fullerenes (e.g. \(C_{60}\)) are hollow cage-like molecules.

Nanoparticles

Nanoparticles have dimensions in the range of roughly 1 to 100 nanometres (nm) and contain between a few hundred and a few thousand atoms. At this scale, materials often behave very differently from how they behave in bulk form. This is because nanoparticles have a very large surface area to volume ratio compared to bulk materials. A larger surface area means more atoms are exposed at the surface, which can dramatically alter reactivity, optical properties and electrical behaviour.

There are several established uses of nanoparticles. Silver nanoparticles are incorporated into some wound dressings and antibacterial coatings because silver at the nanoscale has greater antibacterial effectiveness than bulk silver. Titanium dioxide nanoparticles are used in some sunscreen formulations because they provide UV protection while remaining transparent to visible light, unlike larger particles which appear white. Nanoparticles of various metals and metal oxides are used as catalysts in industrial processes because their large surface area increases reaction rate.

Because nanoparticles are new materials, our knowledge of their long-term effects on health and the environment is still limited. Their very small size means they can potentially enter cells, tissues and even the bloodstream in ways that larger particles cannot. Some research suggests that certain nanoparticles may cause inflammation or other harmful effects in the body or in ecosystems, but long-term data are still being gathered. This is a genuine scientific uncertainty — it does not mean nanoparticles are definitely harmful, but it does mean decisions about their use must weigh potential benefits (improved performance, new medicines) against possible risks (unknown health or ecological impacts). This type of risk-benefit analysis under uncertainty is an important part of how science informs decision-making about new technologies.

Polymers and Metals

Polymers are very long chain molecules. Strong covalent bonds hold the chain together; weaker intermolecular forces act between the chains. Their properties vary depending on the repeating unit and whether the chains are cross-linked or not. Thermoplastic polymers can be remoulded on heating because the intermolecular forces between chains are overcome. Thermosetting polymers cannot be remoulded because they have extensive cross-links between chains. Metals have high melting points, are malleable and are good conductors of electricity and heat. These properties all arise from the sea of delocalised electrons within the metal lattice. Alloys — mixtures of metals — often have different properties from the pure metals they contain, because the differently-sized atoms disrupt the regular lattice and prevent layers sliding as easily.
exam_tip_html: When explaining properties in terms of structure, always link each property to a specific structural feature. For ionic solids: “strong electrostatic forces between many ions require a lot of energy to break — high melting point.” For simple molecules: “weak intermolecular forces between molecules are easily overcome — low melting point.” A very common error is saying the covalent bonds in simple molecules are weak — the bonds within the molecule are strong; it is the forces between molecules that are weak. For nanoparticle questions, always include the large surface area to volume ratio as the reason for their distinct properties.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Giant ionic lattices: high melting points (strong electrostatic forces), conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, brittle. Simple molecular substances: low melting points (weak intermolecular forces between molecules), never conduct. Giant covalent structures: very high melting points (many strong covalent bonds).
  • Carbon allotropes: diamond (4 bonds per atom, very hard, non-conductor); graphite (3 bonds per atom, delocalised electrons, conducts electricity, soft); graphene (single graphite layer, exceptionally strong, conducts); fullerenes (hollow cage molecules, e.g. C60).
  • Nanoparticles (1–100 nm) have a very large surface area to volume ratio, giving them different and often enhanced properties compared to bulk materials. Uses include antibacterial coatings and sunscreens, but long-term health and environmental effects are still being researched.

practice_questions.text:
Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
A) Graphite has ionic bonds but diamond has covalent bonds
B) Graphite has delocalised electrons that can move freely, but diamond uses all outer electrons in covalent bonds
C) Diamond has a higher melting point than graphite
D) Graphite has a giant structure but diamond is a simple molecule
practice_questions.marks: B) Graphite has delocalised electrons that can move freely, but diamond uses all outer electrons in covalent bonds [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the size range (in nanometres) of a nanoparticle.
practice_questions.marks: Roughly 1 to 100 nm (nanometres). Accept answers specifying approximately this range. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of graphite and explain why it is used as a lubricant.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Graphite has flat hexagonal layers of carbon atoms. The layers are held by weak intermolecular forces and can slide over each other easily, making it useful as a lubricant.
Secure: Identifies layered structure and explains sliding.
Developing: Mentions layers but does not link to sliding/lubricant property.
Emerging: Vague description of graphite structure without explaining the lubricant property.

practice_questions.text: Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points but simple molecular compounds have low melting points.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Ionic compounds have strong electrostatic forces of attraction between many oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice. A large amount of energy is needed to break all these forces. Simple molecular compounds have weak intermolecular forces between small molecules; little energy is needed to overcome these, so they melt at low temperatures. The strong covalent bonds within the molecules are not broken on melting.
Secure: Both types explained with reference to the forces broken during melting.
Developing: Correct for one type only; the other is incomplete or refers to breaking covalent bonds for simple molecules.
Emerging: States that one has a high melting point and the other a low one without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Titanium dioxide nanoparticles are used in sunscreen. The surface area of 1 g of titanium dioxide nanoparticles is much greater than 1 g of bulk titanium dioxide powder. Explain why the large surface area to volume ratio makes nanoparticles more effective in sunscreen.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Large surface area to volume ratio means a greater proportion of the atoms are on the surface and available to interact with UV radiation [1]. This means nanoparticles absorb or scatter UV more effectively per gram than bulk powder [1]. Nanoparticles are small enough to be transparent to visible light so sunscreen appears colourless [1]. Overall, less material is needed to achieve the same UV protection, making nanoparticle sunscreens more efficient [1].
Secure: Surface area to volume ratio linked to greater UV interaction and transparency; three of four marking points.
Developing: Mentions large surface area but explanation of effectiveness is incomplete.
Emerging: States nanoparticles are smaller without explaining why this improves performance.

practice_questions.text: Silver nanoparticles are added to some wound dressings to reduce infection. Evaluate the use of silver nanoparticles in medical applications, considering both the benefits and possible risks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Benefits: silver at nanoscale has greater antibacterial activity per gram (large surface area to volume ratio allows more atoms to interact with bacteria); effective against a broad range of bacteria; may reduce reliance on antibiotics. Risks: nanoparticles are small enough to enter cells and tissues; long-term health effects not fully understood; potential for environmental accumulation if silver nanoparticles are washed into water systems; antibacterial resistance to silver is a concern. Conclusion: balances the medical benefits (reduced infection, faster healing) against genuine scientific uncertainty about long-term effects, arguing that continued research and risk monitoring are important.
Secure: At least two benefits and two risks given; some evaluation reaching a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Benefits and risks listed but evaluation is limited.
Emerging: Only benefits or only risks discussed, with no balanced evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which property of nanoparticles explains why they are more reactive than the same material in bulk form?
options: They have a smaller number of atoms
They have a larger surface area to volume ratio
They are made of a different element

knowledge_checks.q: When does an ionic compound conduct electricity?
options: Only when it is a gas
When molten or dissolved in water

knowledge_checks.q: Simple molecular substances have low melting points because the _____ forces between molecules are weak and easily overcome.
Graphite conducts electricity because it has _____ electrons that are free to move within each layer.
Match each carbon allotrope to its key structural feature:
right: Each carbon bonded to four others in a rigid tetrahedral lattice
Flat hexagonal layers with delocalised electrons that can conduct electricity
A single layer of graphite, one atom thick

flashcard_questions.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
flashcard_questions.a: Many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions require a lot of energy to break.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do ionic solids not conduct electricity?
flashcard_questions.a: The ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move to carry charge.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting points?
flashcard_questions.a: Only weak intermolecular forces between molecules need to be overcome — not the covalent bonds within them.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a giant covalent structure?
flashcard_questions.a: An enormous network of atoms all bonded by strong covalent bonds throughout, giving very high melting points.

flashcard_questions.q: How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in diamond?
flashcard_questions.a: Four bonds, arranged in a rigid tetrahedral structure.
One electron per carbon atom is delocalised within each layer and free to move, carrying charge.
A single layer of graphite — one atom thick, very strong, and an excellent conductor.
A hollow, football-shaped molecule of 60 carbon atoms (C60).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the size range of a nanoparticle?
Why are nanoparticles potentially more reactive than bulk materials?
flashcard_questions.a: They have a very large surface area to volume ratio, exposing more atoms at the surface.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one use of silver nanoparticles.
flashcard_questions.a: Antibacterial coatings or wound dressings (accept medical applications).

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the long-term safety of nanoparticles uncertain?
flashcard_questions.a: They are small enough to enter cells and tissues; long-term health and environmental effects are still being studied.

glossary_terms.definition: Compounds made of positive and negative ions held in a regular three-dimensional lattice by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
Substances made of small molecules held together by strong covalent bonds within each molecule, but with only weak forces between the molecules.
Weak attractive forces between molecules that determine physical properties such as melting point and boiling point.
Enormous networks of atoms all bonded by strong covalent bonds extending in all directions, giving very high melting points.
Different structural forms of the same element, with different physical properties because of different bonding arrangements.
Particles with dimensions between roughly 1 and 100 nanometres, containing a few hundred to a few thousand atoms, which can have different properties from the same material in bulk form.
Very long chain molecules made of many small repeating units joined by covalent bonds.
